item.title: Theoretical Contributions to Advance the Business and Society Debate
item.content:encoded:
Jay Joseph, American University of Beirut

Harry Van Buren III, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga

Jennifer Oetzel, American University

Angelika Rettberg, Universidad de los Andes

Global peace is needed now more than ever, yet "peace" still fails to feature in mainstream business and society debates. For over 20 years, "business and peace" has led this debate in business and management studies. Business and peace has generated a broad array of research studies that link business activity to peacebuilding; however, the high volume of descriptive, case-based, and practice-based research in the field, combined with the growing number of parallel contributions to conflict and peace-related topics in general management studies, presents challenges for moving a coherent debate on peace and business forward.

Business and peace is a sub-field of business and management studies with origins dating back to the turn of the millennium. The field historically adopted a positive view toward the role that business can play in conflict zones, promoting a series of aspirational and strategically oriented activities that businesses can adopt to drive peace. From this starting point, the field has fragmented into several different areas, with various studies largely failing to speak to or build upon one another. The end result has been a field that has little epistemological coherence or consistent line of inquiry.

Despite over 20 years of progress being made on the topic, the fragmentation of research and inability to advance a consistent research agenda have undermined the field's ability to move "peace" into mainstream business and society debates. Several field-specific factors present opportunities to advance research: porous field boundaries due to the complexity of this research phenomenon and multidisciplinary array of contributions; and theoretical stagnation, as most research in business and peace has been descriptive, case-based, or practice-based, with the theoretical base of the field remaining shallow.

This special issue for Business & Society seeks to clarify the boundaries and central claims of the business and peace field as well as encourage scholarship that advances theoretical development within it. Recognizing that peace research in business requires contributions from business and management scholars alongside those from political science, international relations, development, and law, this special issue will encourage high-quality interdisciplinary scholarship that either advances existing theoretical frames used in business and peace or presents new ones. The special issue provides a platform for greater participation in business and peace, which aims to advance efforts to move "peace" into mainstream business and society debates.

Potential topics

  • Stakeholder-based theories associated with business and peace
  • Systems perspectives on business and peace
  • Intergroup and contact theories in business contexts
  • Business and human rights frameworks
  • Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and political CSR
  • Governance processes in business and peace
  • Organizing processes and organization studies
  • Normative and ethical frameworks addressing corruption and corporate misconduct
  • International business frameworks in conflict settings
  • Entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial models for conflict-resolution and peace
  • Advanced conceptual development for conflict and peace research
  • Boundary work to clarify field domains in business and peace
  • Theoretical consolidation and advancement of business and peace foundations
